**Relevant context:** Anthropic 2026: 500+ vulnerabilities in production codebases. AIxCC: C and Java evaluated. Embedded systems (C, assembly, RTOS) not evaluated in published AI vulnerability research.

# Replicating LLM Code Review on Multi-Language Projects (Polyglot Codebases)

**Problem:** LLM vulnerability detection is typically evaluated on single-language codebases. Real-world projects often span multiple languages (e.g., Python backend + JavaScript frontend + SQL). Detection rates on polyglot codebases are unknown.

**Direction:** Select 10 full-stack open-source projects with known CVEs spanning at least two languages. Run AI vulnerability scanners on the full codebase. Measure: detection rate per language layer, cross-language vulnerability detection (e.g., SQL injection spanning Python and SQL), and false positive rate.

**Why it matters:** Cross-language vulnerabilities (e.g., injection chains) may be missed by tools that analyze each language in isolation. This is a realistic and under-studied scenario.

**Relevant context:** LLMs in Software Security survey (arXiv 2502.07049): single-language evaluation dominates. Real-world applications are polyglot. Cross-language vulnerability analysis is not evaluated.

# Replicating DARPA AIxCC-Style Vulnerability Detection on a Low-Resource Budget

**Problem:** DARPA AIxCC teams had large resources. The winning team cost ~$152 per task at competition scale. Can AIxCC-style vulnerability detection be replicated at student-scale cost (< $50 total API spend)?

**Direction:** Select 10 synthetic vulnerability scenarios inspired by AIxCC challenge design (memory corruption, logic flaws, injection). Implement a minimal AI-assisted detection pipeline using Claude or GPT-4o API with strict token budgeting. Measure detection rate vs. cost. Compare to AIxCC results.

**Why it matters:** If high-quality vulnerability detection requires large resources, small defenders (open-source projects, NGOs, small companies) cannot benefit from AI defense. Demonstrating low-cost equivalents democratizes defense.

**Relevant context:** DARPA AIxCC 2025: $152/task average cost. SoK AIxCC paper (arXiv 2602.07666). Trail of Bits Buttercup architecture. Student-scale replication not attempted.

# Replicating AI Vulnerability Detection Across Model Families (Open vs. Closed)

**Problem:** Published AI vulnerability detection results primarily use Claude or GPT-4o. Open-source models (Llama 3, Mistral, DeepSeek) may have different performance and safety properties.

**Direction:** Run a fixed vulnerability detection benchmark (30 CVEs across three classes) on three open-source LLMs and two closed-source LLMs. Compare detection rate, false positive rate, explanation quality, and jailbreak resistance to offensive prompting. Analyze safety-performance trade-offs.

**Why it matters:** Open-source models can be fine-tuned to remove safety controls. Understanding their baseline security capabilities and safety properties informs deployment decisions.

**Relevant context:** Jailbreak success rates: 90-99% on open-weight models (TechRxiv 2026). AI vulnerability detection benchmarks focus on proprietary models. Open-source model performance on defensive tasks not systematically evaluated.

# Experiment Variation: Varying Prompt Engineering Strategies for Vulnerability Detection

**Problem:** AI vulnerability detection performance varies with prompting strategy, but no systematic comparison exists across security-relevant prompting techniques.

**Direction:** Run a factorial experiment: 5 prompt strategies (zero-shot, chain-of-thought, few-shot, role-playing as security auditor, adversarial prompt) × 3 LLMs × 20 CVEs. Measure detection rate, false positive rate, explanation quality. Report which prompt strategy maximizes defense-relevant metrics.

**Why it matters:** Even without model changes, better prompting could significantly improve AI-assisted defense. This is immediately actionable for practitioners.

**Relevant context:** Zero-shot accuracy 37.4% → 57-62% with security instructions and few-shot (MDPI 2025). Systematic prompt strategy comparison for vulnerability detection not published.

# Experiment Variation: Varying Code Granularity in AI Vulnerability Scanning (File vs. Function vs. Line)

**Problem:** AI vulnerability scanners can be given varying granularities of code context. Optimal context window size for detection is not characterized.

**Direction:** Run the same AI vulnerability scanner on the same 20 vulnerable code samples at three context granularities: individual function, file-level, and cross-file (with imports/dependencies). Measure detection rate and false positive rate per granularity. Compute cost-performance trade-off.

**Why it matters:** Context granularity affects both detection performance and API cost. Understanding the optimal granularity enables cost-effective deployment.

**Relevant context:** LLM context window size impacts performance (general ML literature). Security-specific optimal context granularity not studied. LLMs in Vulnerability Detection survey (arXiv 2502.07049).

# Experiment Variation: Effect of Code Documentation Quality on AI Vulnerability Detection

**Problem:** Real codebases vary widely in documentation quality. AI scanners may perform better on well-documented code. This interaction has not been studied.

**Direction:** Take 20 vulnerable code samples. Create three versions: (a) original, (b) with added documentation/comments describing intent, (c) with comments removed. Run the same AI scanner on all versions. Measure detection rate and explanation quality as a function of documentation level.

**Why it matters:** If detection quality degrades on poorly documented legacy code, this is precisely where vulnerabilities are most likely to hide. Understanding this interaction guides scanner deployment.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic 2026: vulnerabilities undetected for decades in production codebases (often legacy code with sparse documentation). LLM code understanding vs. code generation literature distinguishes documentation effects but not for security.

# Experiment Variation: Single-Turn vs. Multi-Turn AI Security Analysis

**Problem:** AI vulnerability analysis can be conducted in a single prompt or through iterative multi-turn dialogue (analyst asks follow-up questions). Multi-turn analysis may improve detection quality but at higher cost.

**Direction:** Design a single-turn vulnerability detection protocol and a multi-turn (3-round) protocol. Run both on 20 CVEs with an LLM. Measure: detection rate, false positive rate, explanation quality, and token cost. Compute efficiency frontier.

**Why it matters:** ALOHA's 3-hour vs. weeks advantage may partly reflect multi-turn reasoning. Understanding the cost-benefit of multi-turn analysis enables optimal deployment.

**Relevant context:** ALOHA (PNNL/Anthropic 2026) uses multi-step reasoning chains. AIxCC systems also use multi-step analysis. Direct comparison of single vs. multi-turn security analysis not published.

# Experiment Variation: Effect of Vulnerability Age on AI Detection Performance

**Problem:** AI models are trained on data with a knowledge cutoff. Vulnerabilities discovered after the cutoff may be harder to detect. The relationship between CVE disclosure date and AI detection performance is not studied.

**Direction:** Select 30 CVEs: 10 pre-2022 (before typical LLM training), 10 from 2022-2024, 10 from 2025. Run the same LLM on all without providing CVE IDs. Measure detection rate by age cohort. Test whether newer vulnerabilities are systematically harder to detect.

**Why it matters:** If AI defenders cannot detect recent vulnerability patterns, the newest and most actively exploited vulnerabilities are precisely the ones AI defense fails on.

**Relevant context:** LLM knowledge cutoff effects are studied in general (benchmark contamination literature) but not specifically for vulnerability detection performance by CVE age.

# Experiment Variation: Comparing AI Vulnerability Scanning on First-Party vs. Third-Party Code

**Problem:** AI scanners may perform differently on original first-party code vs. third-party dependencies. Supply chain vulnerabilities often reside in dependencies.

**Direction:** For 15 open-source projects with known CVEs in their dependencies: run AI scanner on (a) first-party code only, (b) dependency code only, (c) full project. Measure detection rate per category. Determine if AI performance is systematically lower for dependency vulnerabilities.

**Why it matters:** Supply chain attacks exploit dependency vulnerabilities. If AI defense tools are worse at detecting them, defenders are blind to the most dangerous attack vector.

**Relevant context:** Supply chain attack proliferation (OWASP 2025, Bastion 2026). LLM vulnerability scanning research focuses on single-project code. Dependency-vs-first-party comparison not studied.

# Experiment Variation: Effect of Model Temperature on Vulnerability Detection Consistency

**Problem:** LLM outputs are stochastic. At high temperature, the same vulnerable code may be judged safe or unsafe across runs. Consistency of AI security verdicts is not characterized.

**Direction:** Run the same 20 vulnerability detection prompts at temperature 0, 0.5, and 1.0 using the same LLM. For each (sample, temperature) combination, run N=10 trials. Measure: verdict consistency rate, false positive rate variance, explanation consistency. Report optimal temperature for stable security verdicts.

**Why it matters:** Inconsistent AI security verdicts undermine defender trust and create audit problems. Characterizing temperature effects enables practitioners to configure tools correctly.

**Relevant context:** LLM temperature effects studied in general but not specifically for security verdict consistency. AI penetration testing guide 2026 notes non-determinism as a challenge but offers no empirical data.

# Experiment Variation: Measuring AI Vulnerability Detection Under Code Review Time Pressure

**Problem:** Real-world code review happens under time pressure. AI scanners may perform differently when configured with token limits that simulate fast-scan vs. deep-scan modes.

**Direction:** Configure AI scanner with three token budget limits (tight = 500 tokens per sample, medium = 2000, unlimited). Run on 20 CVEs. Measure detection rate, false positive rate, explanation completeness. Compute cost-performance Pareto frontier.

**Why it matters:** Practitioners must choose between fast/cheap scans and thorough/expensive ones. Empirical data on this trade-off is absent from the literature.

**Relevant context:** AIxCC: ~$152/task. Mozilla Firefox: $4000 API credits for exploit generation attempt. Cost-performance data for detection (not exploitation) not published.

# Follow-Up to 500+ Vulnerabilities Finding: Which Vulnerability Classes Were Overrepresented?

**Problem:** Claude found 500+ vulnerabilities in production codebases. The class distribution of these vulnerabilities (memory safety, injection, logic, cryptography) is not published. Understanding whether AI detectors have class-specific biases is a natural follow-up.

**Direction:** Replicate a small version of the Anthropic experiment: scan 10 large open-source codebases using a fixed LLM. Categorize found vulnerabilities by CWE class. Compare class distribution to (a) NVD class distribution for the same codebases, (b) prior fuzzing-found vulnerability class distributions.

**Why it matters:** Class-biased AI detection means certain vulnerability types systematically evade AI defense. Understanding the bias directs future tool development.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic 2026: 500+ vulnerabilities. Class distribution not published. NVD provides ground-truth class distributions for many codebases. AIxCC SoK paper (arXiv 2602.07666) analyzes challenge design but not class distribution of AI findings.

# Follow-Up to 22 Firefox Vulnerabilities: Were Any Missed by AI That Were Later Found by Humans?

**Problem:** The Mozilla experiment found 22 Firefox vulnerabilities. It is unclear whether subsequent human review or fuzzing found additional vulnerabilities that the AI missed, which would characterize the false negative rate.

**Direction:** Analyze Mozilla's public CVE/bug database for Firefox vulnerabilities reported after the Anthropic collaboration period. For any new vulnerability found in code that was scanned, retroactively test whether the AI scanner misses it on the same version. Estimate AI false negative rate.

**Why it matters:** False negative rates in AI vulnerability detection are as important as detection rates. This follow-up would provide the missing half of the performance picture.

**Relevant context:** Mozilla + Anthropic 2026: 22 vulnerabilities found. Firefox bug tracker is public. Follow-up false negative analysis not published.

# Follow-Up to Finding>>Exploiting Asymmetry: Does the Asymmetry Hold Under Iterative AI Prompting?

**Problem:** The Mozilla finding showed only 2/22 exploits generated in a single-pass attempt ($4000 API spend). It is unknown whether iterative, multi-turn exploit refinement narrows the asymmetry.

**Direction:** Take 5 known simple vulnerabilities (publicly disclosed with PoC). Attempt exploit generation with a fixed LLM under three conditions: (a) single-turn, (b) 3-turn iterative refinement, (c) 10-turn with feedback. Measure exploit success rate per condition. Assess whether the asymmetry narrows under iterative prompting.

**Why it matters:** If iterative prompting closes the finding>>exploiting gap, current safety assumptions based on single-pass exploit failure may be too optimistic.

**Relevant context:** Mozilla + Anthropic 2026: 2/22 exploits, single-pass. OpenAI Aardvark: multi-step agentic approach. The effect of iterative refinement on exploit generation is not characterized in the literature.

# Follow-Up to DARPA AIxCC 37%→86% Jump: What Architectural Changes Drove the Improvement?

**Problem:** AIxCC vulnerability detection improved from 37% to 86% in one year. The SoK paper describes architectures but does not attribute the performance jump to specific design decisions.

**Direction:** Analyze the published SoK AIxCC paper (arXiv 2602.07666) and team write-ups from Trail of Bits (Buttercup) to extract architectural components. Design a small ablation experiment: implement a minimal CRS with and without the highest-impact component (hypothesize based on analysis). Test on a public CVE benchmark. Measure performance delta.

**Why it matters:** Understanding what drove the performance jump enables targeted improvement and informs what components should be prioritized in future defensive systems.

**Relevant context:** AIxCC SoK (arXiv 2602.07666). Trail of Bits Buttercup writeup. Team Atlanta victory analysis (OODA Loop 2025). Attribution of improvement to specific components not published.

# Follow-Up to AI SOC Automation Claims: Validating the 8x Detection Speed Improvement

**Problem:** Agentic SOC platforms claim 8x faster detection. These claims are vendor-reported and not independently validated. Understanding whether the improvement persists on diverse incident types is a natural follow-up.

**Direction:** Use a public SOC simulation dataset (e.g., DARPA Transparent Computing, CICIDS2017) to compare time-to-detection between: (a) rule-based baseline, (b) LLM-assisted triage. Measure time-to-correct-escalation for three incident types (intrusion, malware, phishing). Compute speedup ratios per incident type.

**Why it matters:** Vendor-reported speedup claims need independent validation. If speedup is incident-type-dependent, relying on AI for all SOC workflows may miss certain threat classes.

**Relevant context:** AI SOC Automation guide 2026 (UnderDefense): 8x detection speedup claim. CICIDS2017 and similar public SOC datasets are accessible. Independent validation of AI SOC performance not found in peer-reviewed literature.

# Follow-Up to LLM-Enhanced Fuzzing: Does AI Seed Generation Actually Improve Coverage on Security-Critical Paths?

**Problem:** LLM-enhanced fuzzing (PromeFuzz, ChatAFL) shows coverage improvements in general. It is not established whether these improvements specifically cover security-critical code paths (not just coverage in general).

**Direction:** Run standard AFL++ and LLM-enhanced fuzzing (using a GPT-4o-guided seed generator) on 5 open-source C libraries with known CVEs. Measure: (a) general code coverage, (b) coverage of security-critical paths (identified by security annotations or manual review), (c) vulnerability detection rate. Compare security-critical coverage vs. general coverage improvement.

**Why it matters:** Higher general coverage may not translate to better vulnerability discovery if AI seeds avoid security-critical paths. This follow-up would reveal whether LLM-fuzzing improves security outcomes specifically.

**Relevant context:** PromeFuzz: 1.5x-3.88x branch coverage improvement (ACM CCS 2025). ChatAFL: 5.8-6.7% code coverage improvement (NDSS). Neither measures security-critical path coverage specifically.

# Novel Direction: AI-Assisted Security Requirement Elicitation for Open Source Projects

**Problem:** Open-source projects often lack explicit security requirements. Vulnerabilities may reflect missing requirements as much as implementation errors. AI could assist in eliciting implicit security requirements from code and documentation.

**Direction:** For 10 open-source projects with known CVEs, use an LLM to infer implicit security requirements from source code, documentation, and commit history. Compare inferred requirements to requirements explicitly violated by each CVE. Measure: what fraction of CVEs reflect requirement violations that the AI could have predicted?

**Why it matters:** Proactive security requirement elicitation could prevent vulnerabilities before implementation, not just detect them after. This is a novel upstream defense.

**Relevant context:** FormaliSE 2026 covers AI in formal requirements. Security requirement elicitation using LLMs is not a studied application area despite clear feasibility.

# Novel Direction: Differential Security Analysis Using Multiple AI Models as a Team

**Problem:** Individual AI models have consistent blind spots. Using multiple models and comparing their findings could identify vulnerabilities that any single model misses.

**Direction:** Run three AI models (Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini) independently on 20 vulnerable code samples. Compute: agreement rate, disagreement patterns, and whether the union of all three models' findings covers more vulnerabilities than any individual model. Measure the marginal detection gain from adding each model.

**Why it matters:** If models have complementary blind spots, ensemble approaches could dramatically improve defensive coverage. This is an actionable insight for deployers.

**Relevant context:** Ensemble methods in ML are well-established. Multi-model security analysis as a deliberate defensive strategy has not been studied. Published AI vulnerability detection research uses single models.

# Novel Direction: AI-Assisted Security Debt Quantification

**Problem:** Technical debt is a software engineering concept for deferred maintenance. Security debt — accumulated vulnerabilities and weaknesses not yet addressed — lacks a quantitative measure. AI could enable automated security debt scoring.

**Direction:** Define a security debt metric: weighted sum of (vulnerability severity × age × exploitability × patch availability). Use an LLM to compute this metric for 10 open-source projects. Validate by correlating security debt score with subsequent breach/CVE history. Compute inter-rater reliability of AI-generated scores.

**Why it matters:** Quantifying security debt enables prioritization and resource allocation. AI-automated security debt scoring could provide a continuous signal for maintainers.

**Relevant context:** Technical debt quantification is a studied SE research area. Security-specific debt quantification using AI is novel. CVSS scoring provides component inputs but not a debt score.

# Novel Direction: Measuring AI Defensive Capability as a Function of Adversary Sophistication

**Problem:** AI defense tools are typically evaluated against known vulnerabilities. Their performance against adversarially obfuscated code, or against novel attack patterns specifically designed to evade them, is not characterized.

**Direction:** Design a red-team experiment: have one AI model (attacker) generate obfuscated versions of vulnerable code designed to evade detection. Have another AI model (defender) attempt to detect the obfuscated vulnerabilities. Measure detection rate degradation vs. non-obfuscated baseline. Iterate for two obfuscation levels.

**Why it matters:** In practice, sophisticated attackers will attempt to evade AI defenses. This experiment characterizes the robustness of AI defense under adversarial conditions.

**Relevant context:** Adversarial evasion of malware detectors is well-studied. Adversarial evasion of static vulnerability scanners by code obfuscation has not been systematically studied for LLM-based scanners.

# Novel Direction: AI-Assisted Vulnerability Clustering for Systemic Pattern Discovery

**Problem:** Individual vulnerability reports are analyzed in isolation. AI could cluster vulnerabilities across a codebase to reveal systemic patterns (e.g., a recurring insecure API usage pattern) that are more informative than individual findings.

**Direction:** Collect AI-generated vulnerability reports for a large open-source project (e.g., Linux kernel CVEs, OpenSSL CVEs). Use an LLM to cluster reports by root cause. Identify recurring patterns. Measure: how many individual CVEs are explained by each systemic pattern? Compare to manually derived clusters from CVE descriptions.

**Why it matters:** Systemic patterns enable targeted developer education and architectural improvements, not just individual patches. This is a higher-leverage defense than one-off patching.

**Relevant context:** Vulnerability taxonomy efforts exist (MITRE CWE). AI-assisted automatic clustering for systemic root cause analysis at codebase scale has not been studied.

# Novel Direction: Measuring the Security Impact of AI-Assisted Code Review Adoption

**Problem:** Organizations are increasingly adopting AI-assisted code review tools. The effect on their actual security posture (measured by CVE frequency, severity, and fix time) is not studied.

**Direction:** Use the GitHub API to identify repositories that adopted a security scanning tool (Dependabot, CodeQL, Semgrep) at a specific date. Compare CVE frequency and fix time before vs. after adoption, using difference-in-differences with matched control repositories. Measure treatment effect.

**Why it matters:** Policy decisions about mandating AI security tools should be informed by empirical evidence of their effectiveness. This is the causal question underlying all defensive AI investment.

**Relevant context:** Sarma & Fisher 2026 (RAND): argues for benchmark incentives for defensive AI. No causal study of AI security tool adoption effect on CVE outcomes published.

# Novel Direction: Evaluating AI-Assisted Security for AI-Generated Code Specifically

**Problem:** AI-generated code has specific vulnerability patterns (Veracode: 45% vulnerable). AI security tools may perform differently on AI-generated vs. human-written code.

**Direction:** Generate 25 code samples using Copilot/Claude Code for the same functionality. For each, also get a human-written version from open-source. Run AI vulnerability scanners on both versions. Compare: detection rate, false positive rate, vulnerability class distribution. Test whether AI-generated code has different scanner performance.

**Why it matters:** If AI security tools are trained on human-written code, they may be poorly calibrated for AI-generated code, precisely where new vulnerabilities are being introduced fastest.

**Relevant context:** Veracode 2025: AI introduces vulnerabilities 45% of the time. AI security scanning calibration for AI-generated code is not studied. This is a novel and increasingly important deployment scenario.

# Novel Direction: Characterizing AI Defensive Capability Across Security Maturity Levels

**Problem:** AI security tools may provide different marginal value to organizations at different security maturity levels (basic vs. advanced). Organizations with mature security programs may derive less benefit from AI tools.

**Direction:** Using a standardized security maturity rubric (OWASP SAMM or NIST CSF), classify 20 open-source projects by security maturity. For each, measure: existing CVE rate, time-to-patch, and AI scanner detection rate. Test whether AI detection rate correlates with project security maturity.

**Why it matters:** AI tools may be most valuable for low-maturity projects (the most vulnerable) but least likely to be adopted there. Understanding this gap informs targeted deployment strategies.

**Relevant context:** Wavestone AI Cyber Benchmark 2025 assesses AI security maturity. OWASP SAMM is a standard maturity framework. Correlation between project security maturity and AI tool effectiveness not studied.

# Replication: Does LLM-Enhanced Fuzzing Improve Over Standard Fuzzing on Real CVE Rediscovery?

**Problem:** LLM-enhanced fuzzing papers (PromeFuzz, ChatAFL) evaluate on new discovery tasks. Whether they help re-discover known CVEs faster than standard fuzzing is not tested.

**Direction:** Select 10 CVEs with known trigger inputs (from public PoC repositories). Run AFL++ and an LLM-guided fuzzer on the same targets. Measure time-to-rediscovery for each CVE. Compute speedup ratio.

**Why it matters:** CVE rediscovery benchmarks provide a controlled comparison. If LLM-enhanced fuzzing doesn't improve rediscovery time, its advantage may be in novel discovery only, with implications for how to deploy these tools.

**Relevant context:** PromeFuzz (ACM CCS 2025), ChatAFL, CI Spark. CVE re-discovery benchmarks used in fuzzing research (FuzzBench). Direct comparison on CVE rediscovery not published.

# Experiment: Systematic Comparison of AI-Assisted Vulnerability Scanning vs. Traditional SAST on the Same Corpus

**Problem:** AI-based scanners are often compared to each other or to manual review. A direct, controlled comparison to traditional SAST tools (Semgrep, CodeQL) on the same corpus with the same ground truth is not readily available.

**Direction:** Run Semgrep, CodeQL, and an LLM-based scanner (Claude via API) on 30 code samples with known CVEs. Use the same ground truth labels. Measure: detection rate, false positive rate, explanation quality, and cost per finding. Compute complementarity (does LLM find things SAST misses?).

**Why it matters:** Practitioners need to decide whether to add AI scanners alongside existing SAST tools. A controlled comparison with complementarity analysis answers this question directly.

**Relevant context:** MDPI AI vulnerability detection review (2025) notes LLMs vs. SAST comparison is important but not standardized. No head-to-head study with both cost and complementarity analysis found.

# Cross-Domain Transfer: Applying Software Reliability Engineering Failure Rate Models to AI Security Tools

**Problem:** Software reliability engineering (SRE) has formal models (NHPP, Jelinski-Moranda) for predicting software failure rates over time. These could be applied to model AI vulnerability scanner failure (missed detection) rates.

**Direction:** Fit a software reliability growth model to AI vulnerability scanner detection data across model versions (treating each version as a 'testing interval' and missed CVEs as 'failures'). Forecast the detection rate trajectory. Compare model fit to empirical data from published benchmarks.

**Why it matters:** Reliability models could predict when AI defense tools will reach acceptable performance thresholds, informing deployment timelines and investment decisions.

**Relevant context:** SRE models are standard in software quality engineering. Application to AI security tool performance tracking is novel. AIxCC 37%→86% trajectory provides empirical data for model fitting.

# Causal Chain: Intervening on the Human Expertise Bottleneck in AI-Assisted Vulnerability Verification

**Problem:** AI vulnerability scanners generate findings, but verification requires expert judgment. The causal chain: AI finds vuln → expert verifies → patch deployed. The verification bottleneck slows remediation.

**Direction:** Design a tiered verification protocol: (a) AI-only verification (LLM checks its own finding), (b) non-expert CS student verification with AI guidance, (c) expert verification. Run all three on 15 findings. Measure: verification accuracy, time, and cost per tier. Identify the minimum verification tier that achieves acceptable accuracy.

**Why it matters:** If non-experts with AI guidance can accurately verify findings, the verification bottleneck can be broken without expensive expert time. This changes the economics of AI-assisted defense.

**Relevant context:** Qualys Agent Val addresses validation. DARPA AIxCC: $152/task average. Expert verification bottleneck not characterized as a causal link in remediation pipelines.

# Backcast from Standardized AI Defense Evaluation: What Does a Minimal Viable Benchmark Require?

**Problem:** For the community to agree on AI defense evaluation standards, a minimum viable benchmark specification is needed. What properties must it have?

**Direction:** Survey five existing security benchmarks (CAIBench, ExCyTIn-Bench, CyberSOCEval, AutoPatchBench, AIxCC) on the following dimensions: ground truth quality, reproducibility, cost to run, language/domain coverage, defensive focus. Use this analysis to draft a minimum viable benchmark specification for AI-powered defense. Validate the specification against one existing benchmark.

**Why it matters:** Without consensus benchmark properties, evaluation remains fragmented. A published specification enables community convergence.

**Relevant context:** CLAUDE.md open problem: 'No defensive benchmarks equivalent to offensive ones.' CAIBench, ExCyTIn-Bench, CyberSOCEval exist for offense or SOC. Pure defensive benchmark specification not published.

# Compounding Risk: AI Overconfidence + Missing Ground Truth = Undetectable Performance Degradation

**Problem:** Two interacting failures: (1) AI security tools may be overconfident in their outputs (poor calibration); (2) defenders often lack ground truth to verify AI performance in production. The combination means performance can degrade undetected.

**Direction:** Design a monitoring protocol for AI security tool performance without ground truth: use proxy metrics (finding rate stability, explanation consistency across runs, agreement with independent re-analysis). Test the protocol on a simulated degradation scenario (vary model version or prompt). Measure whether the proxy metrics detect performance degradation.

**Why it matters:** Production AI defense tools with no monitoring mechanism may degrade silently. This is a safety-critical governance gap.

**Relevant context:** AI monitoring in production is a general ML ops challenge. Security-specific monitoring without ground truth is novel. Temperature/consistency experiments (see earlier ideas) provide methodological groundwork.

# Measuring AI Vulnerability Detection Performance on Cryptographic Implementation Flaws

**Problem:** Cryptographic implementation vulnerabilities (timing attacks, weak PRNG seeding, padding oracle, etc.) require specialized domain knowledge to detect. AI model performance on this specific class is not characterized.

**Direction:** Collect 15 CVEs from cryptographic libraries (OpenSSL, libsodium, NSS). Run three LLMs on the source code. Measure detection rate and explanation correctness for cryptographic vs. non-cryptographic CVEs from the same libraries. Test whether detection rate differs by class.

**Why it matters:** Cryptographic vulnerabilities are particularly dangerous (break confidentiality at scale) and require specialized knowledge. If AI is worse at finding them, this is a high-risk gap.

**Relevant context:** LLM vulnerability detection benchmarks do not segregate cryptographic implementation vulnerabilities. OpenSSL and similar libraries are well-covered in CVE databases.

# AI-Assisted Threat Modeling: Does Automated STRIDE Analysis Match Expert Analysis?

**Problem:** STRIDE threat modeling is a standard security engineering practice. AI-assisted STRIDE analysis is increasingly proposed but not empirically validated against expert analysis.

**Direction:** For 5 open-source web applications: have an LLM perform STRIDE threat modeling (generate threat list per component), then have a security-knowledgeable human rater evaluate completeness and accuracy vs. a reference threat model. Measure recall (fraction of reference threats found) and precision (fraction of AI threats that are real).

**Why it matters:** If AI threat modeling is accurate, it could provide security analysis to projects that cannot afford security consultants. If not, it may create false assurance.

**Relevant context:** STRIDE is well-documented (Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool). AI threat modeling applications described in practitioner blogs but not empirically validated against expert baselines.

# Calibration Study: Do AI Security Confidence Scores Reflect Actual Exploitability?

**Problem:** AI vulnerability scanners produce confidence scores for their findings, but it is not known whether these scores correlate with actual exploitability (CVSSv3 exploitability subscore).

**Direction:** Run an AI vulnerability scanner on 40 CVEs with known CVSSv3 exploitability scores. Measure Spearman correlation between AI confidence score and CVSSv3 exploitability. Compute calibration curve. Test whether high-confidence AI findings are disproportionately high-exploitability.

**Why it matters:** Well-calibrated confidence scores enable rational prioritization. If AI is overconfident on low-exploitability findings and underconfident on high-exploitability ones, defenders are misinformed.

**Relevant context:** CVSSv3 exploitability metrics are published for most CVEs in NVD. AI scanner confidence calibration to exploitability not studied in the literature.

# Compounding Risk: AI Defense Tool Prompt Injection + Malicious Codebase = Attacker-Controlled Security Reports

**Problem:** Two interacting failures: (1) AI code review tools are vulnerable to prompt injection via malicious comments in code; (2) security reports from these tools are trusted by defenders. Combined, an attacker who controls code under review can manipulate the AI's security report.

**Direction:** Design and test prompt injection attacks targeting an AI code review tool: embed adversarial instructions in code comments or docstrings that cause the AI to (a) omit a real vulnerability from its report, (b) report a false positive in clean code.
